result:
I've been thinking about lists.

Not to-do lists, exactly, though those count. I mean the strange power of the form itself: the way that putting things one under another, with no connective tissue between them, does something that paragraphs can't.

Sei Shōnagon, a lady-in-waiting in tenth-century Japan, kept a notebook full of them. "Things that make one's heart beat faster." "Things that are distant though near." "Elegant things." Under that last one: a white coat worn over a violet waistcoat; duck eggs; shaved ice with liana syrup in a new silver bowl; a rosary of rock crystal; wisteria blossoms; plum blossoms covered with snow; a pretty child eating strawberries.

A thousand years later, that list still works. You read it and you can *feel* her taste—not described, but demonstrated. She never says what elegance is. She just puts seven things next to each other and trusts you to feel the shape of the space they enclose.

That's the trick, I think. A list refuses to explain the relationship between its items. It leaves the connection unstated, and so you have to make it yourself. The wisteria and the duck eggs have nothing in common until you hold them together and ask what they share—and then suddenly you know something about coolness, about pale colors, about a kind of quiet richness. You've done the work, so the knowledge is yours.

Prose argues. A list just points.

There's a version of this in grief, too. When someone dies, people don't usually remember them in essays. They remember in lists. The way he hummed while making coffee. The specific ugly sweater. How she always said "well!" before changing the subject. The items don't add up to a thesis. They're not supposed to. They're a constellation, and the person is the shape you see when you connect the points.

I notice I like lists because they're honest about incompleteness. A paragraph pretends to be whole—it has a beginning and an end, it rounds itself off. A list can always take one more item. It admits that it's a sample, not a census. It says: here are some things, there are more, I stopped here.

Things that are distant though near: the festival of the last day of the twelfth month and the first of the new year. The road between here and someone's house when you've quarreled. The moment just after you've said something you can't take back.

Things that are near though distant: paradise. The course of a boat. The relationship between a man and a woman.

I didn't write those. She did. But I recognize them, which I suppose is the point.
